claims.source: Quantification of severe hypoxia in these two structures revealed significantly worse severe hypoxia in the hippocampus (Figure 1O), likely due to longer seizure durations.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1O comparing hypoxia in hippocampus and neocortex.

claims.claim: Maximal electroconvulsive shock (MES) induced a long-lasting hypoxic event in the hippocampus similar to those observed following spontaneous or electrical kindled seizures.
claims.source: Maximal electroconvulsive shock (MES) which models generalized convulsions (Young et al., 2006) and 3 Hz electrical stimulation, which drives epileptiform activity and behavioral seizures (Teskey and Racine, 1993) both induced a long-lasting hypoxic event in the hippocampus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) similar to those observed following spontaneous or electrical kindled seizures.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to Young et al., 2006 and Teskey and Racine, 1993.

claims.claim: 3 Hz electrical stimulation induced a long-lasting hypoxic event in the hippocampus similar to those observed following spontaneous or electrical kindled seizures.
claims.source: Maximal electroconvulsive shock (MES) which models generalized convulsions (Young et al., 2006) and 3 Hz electrical stimulation, which drives epileptiform activity and behavioral seizures (Teskey and Racine, 1993) both induced a long-lasting hypoxic event in the hippocampus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) similar to those observed following spontaneous or electrical kindled seizures.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to Young et al., 2006 and Teskey and Racine, 1993.

claims.claim: A postictal severe hypoxic event follows epileptiform seizures regardless of the eliciting technique.
claims.source: We conclude that a postictal severe hypoxic event follows epileptiform seizures regardless of the eliciting technique.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from multiple seizure induction methods (spontaneous, kindling, MES, 3 Hz stimulation) all showing postictal hypoxia.

claims.claim: Blood flow increased during afterdischarges.
claims.source: Blood flow increased during afterdischarges, which was consistent with previous observations (Metzger, 1977).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by laser Doppler flowmetry data and a citation to Metzger, 1977.

claims.claim: The postictal severe hypoxia is accompanied by reduced blood flow to 53.0 ± 8.3% relative to baseline between 40 and 60 min post-seizure.
claims.source: Importantly, the postictal severe hypoxia is accompanied by reduced blood flow to 53.0 ± 8.3% relative to baseline between 40 and 60 min post-seizure.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by laser Doppler flowmetry data measuring blood flow changes post-seizure.

claims.claim: Blood flow recovered on a similar time-scale to tissue oxygenation indicating that the postictal severe hypoxia is, in part, related to hypoperfusion.
claims.source: Furthermore, blood flow recovered on a similar time-scale to tissue oxygenation indicating that the postictal severe hypoxia is, in part, related to hypoperfusion.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by concurrent measurements of blood flow and tissue oxygenation showing similar recovery kinetics.

claims.claim: Nifedipine pre-treatment caused an elevation of baseline pO2.
claims.source: We observed higher pO2 levels at baseline (+9.0 mmHg, p<0.01, paired ANOVA), throughout the postictal period, and an earlier return to baseline relative to vehicle (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C comparing baseline pO2 levels with and without nifedipine treatment.

claims.claim: Nifedipine pre-treatment did not alter the afterdischarge duration.
claims.source: Pre-treatment with the L-type calcium channel antagonist nifedipine 30 min prior to seizure elicitation did not alter the afterdischarge duration (Figure 2C) indicating that nifedipine effects can be attributed to a neurovascular mechanism.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C comparing seizure durations with and without nifedipine treatment.

claims.claim: Nifedipine pre-treatment significantly attenuated the area below the severe hypoxic threshold (pO2 < 10 mmHg).
claims.source: Moreover, nifedipine pre-treatment significantly attenuated the area below the severe hypoxic threshold (pO2 < 10 mmHg) (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D comparing hypoxia severity with and without nifedipine treatment.

claims.claim: Nifedipine was effective at reducing postictal severe hypoxia when administered immediately following termination of the afterdischarge.
claims.source: We also observed that nifedipine was effective at reducing postictal severe hypoxia when administered immediately following termination of the afterdischarge (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B comparing hypoxia with post-seizure nifedipine administration.

claims.claim: L-type calcium channels play a key role in the tonic phase of vascular smooth muscle contraction.
claims.source: This is not surprising since L-type calcium channels play a key role in the tonic phase of vascular smooth muscle contraction (Putney and McKay, 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Putney and McKay, 1999.

claims.claim: 2 min of 3 Hz stimulation resulted in a remarkably similar profile of severe hypoxia compared to the standard 1 s stimulation evoked afterdischarges in young freely moving rats.
claims.source: In young (P25-P40) freely moving rats, we first determined that 2 min of 3 Hz stimulation resulted in a remarkably similar profile of severe hypoxia compared to the standard 1 s stimulation evoked afterdischarges (Figure 2E,F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E,F comparing hypoxia profiles from different stimulation protocols.

claims.claim: Sustained 13.8 ± 4.0% arteriole constriction was observed following 3 Hz stimulation in acute hippocampal slices (60–90 min post-stim).
claims.source: We observed sustained 13.8 ± 4.0% arteriole constriction following stimulation (60–90 min post-stim, Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by direct measurements of arteriole diameter in hippocampal slices shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: A 13.8% reduction in arteriole diameter would lead to blood flow that is 55.2% of baseline according to Poiseuille's law.
claims.source: Poiseuille's law dictates that a 13.8% reduction in diameter would lead to blood flow that is 55.2% of baseline, which correlates well with our laser Doppler flowmetry measurements (53.0 ± 8.3% at 40–60 min, Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on applying Poiseuille's law to the measured arteriole constriction data.

claims.claim: Pretreatment with nifedipine (50 µM) caused significant vessel dilation (108.4 ± 2.9% relative to baseline) in hippocampal slices.
claims.source: Pretreatment with nifedipine (50 µM) caused significant vessel dilation (108.4 ± 2.9% relative to baseline, p<0.05, paired t-test) and prevented 3 Hz stimulation-induced vessel constriction (Figure 2K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2K measuring vessel diameter with nifedipine treatment in hippocampal slices.

claims.claim: Nifedipine pretreatment prevented 3 Hz stimulation-induced vessel constriction in hippocampal slices.
claims.source: Pretreatment with nifedipine (50 µM) caused significant vessel dilation (108.4 ± 2.9% relative to baseline, p<0.05, paired t-test) and prevented 3 Hz stimulation-induced vessel constriction (Figure 2K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2K comparing vessel constriction with and without nifedipine in hippocampal slices.

claims.claim: Severe hypoxia following seizures is mediated by vasoconstriction and hypoperfusion.
claims.source: Our data obtained using laser Doppler flowmetry, nifedipine treatment, and arteriole constriction in slice all provided convergent evidence that severe hypoxia following seizures is mediated by vasoconstriction and hypoperfusion.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including laser Doppler flowmetry, pharmacological interventions, and direct vessel measurements.

claims.claim: Maximal changes in blood flow were quantified in mL/100 g/min and the brain area where this change occurred was compared to ictal EEG to determine concordance between local hypoperfusion and seizure activity.
claims.source: Maximal changes in blood flow were quantified in mL/100 g/min and the brain area where this change occurred was compared to ictal EEG to determine concordance between local hypoperfusion and seizure activity (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the methodology used in the clinical ASL study.

claims.claim: Maximal postictal cerebral blood flow reductions of at least 10 mL/100 g/min were seen in 8 of 10 subjects.
claims.source: Maximal postictal cerebral blood flow reductions of at least 10 mL/100 g/min were seen in 8 of 10 subjects (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by clinical ASL data from 10 epilepsy patients shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: A mean baseline CBF of 59.0 ± 4.4 mL/100 g/min and mean CBF of 42.1 ± 3.4 mL/100 g/min following seizures was observed in the region of interest for all 10 subjects, for a difference of 16.9 ± 4.1 mL/100 g/min or 26.6 ± 6.0% from baseline.
claims.source: Looking at the region of interest (ROI) for all 10 subjects, we observed a mean baseline CBF of 59.0 ± 4.4 mL/100 g/ and mean CBF of 42.1 ± 3.4 mL/100 g/min following seizures, for a difference of 16.9 ± 4.1 mL/100 g/min or 26.6 ± 6.0% from baseline (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by clinical ASL data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The magnitude of hypoperfusion was positively correlated with seizure duration in epilepsy patients.
claims.source: Furthermore, the magnitude of hypoperfusion was positively correlated with seizure duration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), just as we saw with the magnitude of hypoxia and seizure duration in the rat (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by clinical ASL data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B (note: likely Figure 3—figure supplement 1B based on context).

claims.claim: In the two subjects without observable hypoperfusion of >10 mL/100 g/min, the seizure durations were notably shorter.
claims.source: In the two subjects without observable hypoperfusion of >10 mL/100 g/min, the seizure durations were notably shorter and may account for the absence of hypoperfusion.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observation of clinical data and inference about the relationship between seizure duration and hypoperfusion.

claims.claim: CBF of 65.0 ± 3.6% relative to baseline was observed in the postictal scan when excluding the two patients without hypoperfusion >10 mL/100 g/min.
claims.source: Excluding these two patients, CBF of 65.0 ± 3.6% relative to baseline was observed in the postictal scan.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by clinical ASL data from 8 of 10 patients.

claims.claim: In all eight cases where hypoperfusion >10 mL/100 g/min was observed, the area of maximal hypoperfusion overlapped with a brain structure subjected to seizure activity.
claims.source: In all eight cases where hypoperfusion >10 mL/100 g/min was observed, we noted that the area of maximal hypoperfusion overlapped with a brain structure subjected to seizure activity (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by clinical data comparing ASL hypoperfusion maps with EEG localization of seizure activity shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: Hypoperfusion is specifically localized to those areas involved in the seizure and is a local phenomenon.
claims.source: Thus, hypoperfusion is specifically localized to those areas involved in the seizure and is indeed a local phenomenon.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by clinical data showing concordance between hypoperfusion and seizure localization.

claims.claim: COX-2 is expressed throughout the rat brain with particularly dense expression in neurons of the hippocampus.
claims.source: COX-2 is expressed throughout the rat brain (Figure 4A) with particularly dense expression in neurons of the hippocampus (Figure 4B–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claims.claim: COX-2 plays a well-established role in neurovascular coupling.
claims.source: This expression profile and the well-established role in neurovascular coupling (Niwa et al., 2000; Lecrux et al., 2011; Lacroix et al., 2015) made COX-2 a likely candidate responsible for postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Niwa et al., 2000; Lecrux et al., 2011; Lacroix et al., 2015.

claims.claim: COX-1 is involved in the tonic control of brain blood flow through astrocyte signaling.
claims.source: We also hypothesized that COX-1 would not play a role since it is involved in the tonic control of brain blood flow through astrocyte signaling (Rosenegger et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rosenegger et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Celecoxib prevented postictal severe hypoxia.
claims.source: Neither drug had any significant effect on afterdischarge duration and as predicted, celecoxib (Figure 4E,F), but not SC-560 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), prevented postictal severe hypoxia.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E,F comparing hypoxia with and without celecoxib treatment.

claims.claim: SC-560 did not prevent postictal severe hypoxia.
claims.source: Neither drug had any significant effect on afterdischarge duration and as predicted, celecoxib (Figure 4E,F), but not SC-560 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), prevented postictal severe hypoxia.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B showing no effect of SC-560 on hypoxia.

claims.claim: Neither celecoxib nor SC-560 had any significant effect on afterdischarge duration.
claims.source: Neither drug had any significant effect on afterdischarge duration and as predicted, celecoxib (Figure 4E,F), but not SC-560 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), prevented postictal severe hypoxia.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing seizure durations with and without drug treatment.

claims.claim: Pre-administration of acetaminophen dose-dependently inhibited severe hypoxia without altering afterdischarge duration.
claims.source: Indeed, pre-administration of acetaminophen dose-dependently inhibited severe hypoxia without altering afterdischarge duration (Figure 4G,H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G,H comparing hypoxia at different acetaminophen doses.

claims.claim: Administering acetaminophen immediately following termination of the afterdischarge had no effect on the postictal hypoxic profile.
claims.source: Unlike nifedipine, administering acetaminophen immediately following termination of the afterdischarge had no effect on the postictal hypoxic profile (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D comparing hypoxia with post-seizure acetaminophen administration.

claims.claim: COX-2 activity during the afterdischarge gives rise to prolonged postictal severe hypoxia.
claims.source: Since acetaminophen had to be present at the time of the afterdischarge, this suggests that COX-2 activity during the afterdischarge gives rise to prolonged postictal severe hypoxia.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that acetaminophen must be present during the seizure to be effective.

claims.claim: Acetaminophen prevented vessel constriction following 3 Hz stimulation in hippocampal slices.
claims.source: Indeed, acetaminophen prevented vessel constriction following stimulation (Figure 4I), but unlike nifedipine (Figure 2K), had no effect on vessel diameter prior to stimulation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4I measuring vessel diameter with acetaminophen treatment in hippocampal slices.

claims.claim: Acetaminophen had no effect on vessel diameter prior to stimulation in hippocampal slices.
claims.source: Indeed, acetaminophen prevented vessel constriction following stimulation (Figure 4I), but unlike nifedipine (Figure 2K), had no effect on vessel diameter prior to stimulation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4I comparing vessel diameter before and after stimulation with acetaminophen treatment.

claims.claim: PTGS2Y385F mice have a single amino acid substitution in cyclooxygenase active site, have intact peroxidase function, and have blunted prostanoid production in response to LPS.
claims.source: Specifically, these mice (PTGS2Y385F) have a single amino acid substitution in cyclooxygenase active site, have intact peroxidase function, and have blunted prostanoid production in response to LPS (Yu et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2006 describing the genetic characteristics of the mouse model.

claims.claim: Both PTGS2Y385F mutant and C57BL/6J control mice exhibit brief afterdischarges which did not differ in duration in response to electrical kindling stimulation.
claims.source: Both mutant and C57BL/6J controls exhibit brief afterdischarges, which did not differ in duration in response to electrical kindling stimulation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing seizure durations between mutant and control mice.

claims.claim: Only C57BL/6J controls showed severe hypoxia during the postictal period, while the PTGS2Y385F mutants remained within normoxia.
claims.source: However, only C57BL/6J controls showed severe hypoxia during the postictal period, while the mutants remained within normoxia (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B,C comparing postictal oxygen levels in mutant and control mice.

claims.claim: Severe hypoxia was blocked by acetaminophen pre-treatment in C57BL/6J controls.
claims.source: Furthermore, severe hypoxia was blocked by acetaminophen pre-treatment in C57BL/6J controls corroborating our results in rats and no further effect was seen in COX-2 mutants (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D comparing hypoxia with acetaminophen treatment in control mice.

claims.claim: Acetaminophen had no further effect on postictal hypoxia in COX-2 mutants.
claims.source: Furthermore, severe hypoxia was blocked by acetaminophen pre-treatment in C57BL/6J controls corroborating our results in rats and no further effect was seen in COX-2 mutants (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D showing no additional effect of acetaminophen in mutant mice.

claims.claim: Rho Kinase inhibition with fasudil augmented postictal severe hypoxia perhaps by distributing blood flow to areas outside of the afterdischarge zone.
claims.source: In fact, Rho Kinase inhibition with fasudil achieved the opposite effect and augmented postictal severe hypoxia perhaps by distributing blood flow to areas outside of the afterdischarge zone.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased hypoxia with fasudil treatment, with speculation about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia is not amenable to several vasodilatory treatments.
claims.source: Together, these data provide support for the inflexible nature of postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia, which is not amenable to several vasodilatory treatments, and highlights the central roles COX-2 activation and the sustained calcium elevation in vascular smooth muscle.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from multiple pharmacological interventions showing lack of effect of various vasodilators.

claims.claim: COX-2 activation and sustained calcium elevation in vascular smooth muscle play central roles in postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia.
claims.source: Together, these data provide support for the inflexible nature of postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia, which is not amenable to several vasodilatory treatments, and highlights the central roles COX-2 activation and the sustained calcium elevation in vascular smooth muscle.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from multiple pharmacological interventions targeting COX-2 and calcium channels.

claims.claim: Acute dosing with commonly prescribed ASDs had no significant effect on postictal severe hypoxia when compared to vehicle treatment.
claims.source: Acute dosing with commonly prescribed ASDs had no significant effect on postictal severe hypoxia when compared to vehicle treatment (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Table 4 comparing multiple ASDs.

claims.claim: Ethosuximide reduced the severity of hypoxia by 47.61 ± 11.01%.
claims.source: Interestingly, ethosuximide reduced the severity of hypoxia by 47.61 ± 11.01%.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from ethosuximide treatment experiments.

claims.claim: Ethosuximide is used to treat absence seizures by inhibiting T-type calcium channels, but partial inhibition of L-type calcium channels has been reported.
claims.source: Ethosuximide is used to treat absence seizures by inhibiting T-type calcium channels, but partial inhibition of L-type calcium channels has been reported (Kostyuk et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kostyuk et al., 1992 and established knowledge about ethosuximide.

claims.claim: Pretreatment with nifedipine prevented the expression of postictal severe hypoxia without affecting seizure duration in neocortical seizures.
claims.source: As expected, pretreatment with nifedipine prevented the expression of postictal severe hypoxia without affecting seizure duration (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B comparing neocortical oxygen levels with and without nifedipine treatment.

claims.claim: The vehicle-treated seizure group displayed a significantly shorter hang time at 40 min postictal.
claims.source: Although severely hypoxic at both the 20- and 40 min time-point, the vehicle-treated seizure group displayed a significantly shorter hang time at 40 min postictal (Figure 6C), suggesting that the duration of severe hypoxia is important for the generation of behavioral deficits.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6C from the hanging bar test.

claims.claim: At 80 min post-afterdischarge, the non-treated group's pO2 levels returned to normoxia and the behavioral performance was equivalent to nifedipine treated and non-seizure groups.
claims.source: At 80 min post-afterdischarge, the non-treated group's pO2 levels returned to normoxia and the behavioral performance was equivalent to nifedipine treated and non-seizure groups.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral and oxygen data at 80 min post-seizure.

claims.claim: It is the postictal severe hypoxic period that is responsible for the motor weakness, not the seizure per se.
claims.source: These results indicate that it is the postictal severe hypoxic period that is responsible for the motor weakness, not the seizure per se.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that preventing hypoxia with nifedipine prevents motor weakness despite seizures occurring.

claims.claim: Rats that were severely hypoxic at the time of memory encoding (seizure+vehicle) explored the novel and familiar objects with no significant preference 24 hr later.
claims.source: Rats that were severely hypoxic at the time of memory encoding (seizure+vehicle, Figure 6E) explored the novel and familiar objects with no significant preference 24 hr later, which indicates that they were unable to form the memory during the postictal severe hypoxia (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from the novel object recognition task shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Rats that had seizures without severe hypoxia (acetaminophen pre-treatment) performed at the same level as controls (acetaminophen or vehicle without seizures) in the novel object recognition task.
claims.source: Moreover, the rats that had seizures without severe hypoxia (acetaminophen pre-treatment) performed at the same level as controls (acetaminophen or vehicle without seizures).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from the novel object recognition task.

claims.claim: Severe hypoxia following seizures, and not the seizures themselves, are the underlying cause of postictal memory and motor impairments.
claims.source: These results, along with the ability of nifedipine to prevent Todd's paresis, support the hypothesis that severe hypoxia following seizures, and not the seizures themselves, are the underlying cause of these specific postictal impairments.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral experiments showing that preventing hypoxia prevents behavioral impairments despite seizures occurring.

claims.claim: Brief seizures initiate a local and long-lasting hypoperfusion/hypoxic insult, which is responsible for behavioral dysfunction in the postictal period rather than the seizure itself.
claims.source: Thus, brief seizures initiate a local and long-lasting hypoperfusion/hypoxic insult, which is responsible for behavioral dysfunction in the postictal period rather than the seizure itself.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion supported by multiple lines of evidence from oxygen measurements, blood flow measurements, and behavioral experiments.

claims.claim: Prior to this report the direction of postictal hemodynamic changes was unclear since conflicting reports indicated either postictal hypoperfusion or hyperperfusion.
claims.source: Prior to this report the direction of postictal hemodynamic changes was unclear since conflicting reports indicated either postictal hypoperfusion (Rowe et al., 1991; Newton et al., 1992; Leonhardt et al., 2005) or hyperperfusion (Fong et al., 2000; Tatlidil, 2000; Hassan et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing conflicting results.

claims.claim: The discordance in prior reports of postictal hemodynamic changes is most likely explained by the variable timing of the single postictal scans.
claims.source: This discordance is most likely explained by the variable timing of the single postictal scans.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' findings about the time-course of postictal hypoperfusion.

claims.claim: The most severe hypoxia occurred between 20–60 min post-seizure in rat models.
claims.source: In our rat models we observed the most severe hypoxia occurred between 20–60 min post-seizure thus we performed clinical postictal scans in this time window and observed dramatic local hypoperfusion.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from continuous oxygen measurements in rats.

claims.claim: Only those previous studies that imaged during the 20-60 min postictal period observed hypoperfusion.
claims.source: Importantly, only those previous studies that imaged during this period observed hypoperfusion, which highlights the importance of timing with this phenomenon (Rowe et al., 1991; Newton et al., 1992; Leonhardt et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and inference about the relationship between timing and observations.

claims.claim: The timing of postictal scans is an important consideration as these techniques may aid the ability of clinicians to locate the seizure onset zone in potential surgical candidates.
claims.source: Moreover, the timing of postictal scans is an important consideration as these techniques may aid the ability of clinicians to locate the seizure onset zone in potential surgical candidates (Duncan et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Duncan et al., 1993 and speculation about clinical applications.

claims.claim: Few have investigated local tissue oxygenation during the seizure event itself prior to this study.
claims.source: Prior to this study, few have investigated local tissue oxygenation during the seizure event itself and they identified a transient 'dip' at seizure onset that quickly recovers (Bahar et al., 2006; Suh et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bahar et al., 2006 and Suh et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Previous studies identified a transient 'dip' in oxygenation at seizure onset that quickly recovers.
claims.source: Prior to this study, few have investigated local tissue oxygenation during the seizure event itself and they identified a transient 'dip' at seizure onset that quickly recovers (Bahar et al., 2006; Suh et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bahar et al., 2006 and Suh et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The longest previous oxygen recording included 30 s of postictal oxygen sampling and took place under ketamine anesthesia, which dramatically reduces neurovascular coupling by inhibiting NMDA-dependent COX-2 activation.
claims.source: The longest of these recordings included 30 s of postictal oxygen sampling and took place under ketamine anesthesia, which dramatically reduces neurovascular coupling by inhibiting NMDA-dependent COX-2 activation (Tran and Gordon, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tran and Gordon, 2015.

claims.claim: It is unsurprising that postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia was not identified in previous studies that used ketamine anesthesia.
claims.source: It is therefore unsurprising that postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia was not identified in these studies.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the effects of ketamine on neurovascular coupling.

claims.claim: One group discovered hypoxyprobe-positive neurons following pilocarpine-induced SE and during the period of recurrent spontaneous seizures (three weeks post SE), which they attributed to the hypoxic dip that occurs during seizures.
claims.source: One group discovered hypoxyprobe-positive neurons following pilocarpine-induced SE and during the period of recurrent spontaneous seizures (three weeks post SE), which they attributed to the hypoxic dip that occurs during seizures (Gualtieri et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gualtieri et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The duration of the transient dip in oxygenation at seizure onset is dwarfed by the prolonged period of severe hypoxia during the postictal period and likely accounts for hypoxyprobe labeling.
claims.source: We also observed a transient dip in oxygenation at seizure onset, but the duration of this dip is dwarfed by the prolonged period of severe hypoxia during the postictal period and likely accounts for hypoxyprobe labeling.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparing the magnitude and duration of ictal versus postictal hypoxia.

claims.claim: Activity-dependent induction of COX-2 in neurons plays an important role in normal neurovascular coupling by producing vasoactive prostanoids that act on blood vessel receptors to cause vasodilation.
claims.source: Activity-dependent induction of COX-2 in neurons plays an important role in normal neurovascular coupling by producing vasoactive prostanoids that act on blood vessel receptors to cause vasodilation (Niwa et al., 2000; Lecrux et al., 2011; Lacroix et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Niwa et al., 2000; Lecrux et al., 2011; Lacroix et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Under pathophysiological activation during electrographic seizure activity, vasodilation is quickly switched to prolonged vasoconstriction.
claims.source: Under pathophysiological activation during electrographic seizure activity, we observed that vasodilation is quickly switched to prolonged vasoconstriction.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from blood flow and vessel diameter measurements during and after seizures.

claims.claim: Inhibiting PGE2 synthesis provided partial inhibition of severe hypoxia.
claims.source: We also found that inhibiting PGE2 synthesis provided partial inhibition of severe hypoxia.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from CAY-10526 treatment experiments shown in Table 3.

claims.claim: The EP1 and EP3 receptor subtypes for PGE2 have been observed to induce vasoconstriction and may mediate part of the postictal hypoperfusion response.
claims.source: The EP1 and EP3 receptor subtypes for PGE2 have been observed to induce vasoconstriction (Jadhav et al., 2004) and may mediate part of this response.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jadhav et al., 2004 and speculation about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Nifedipine's inhibition of severe hypoxia even when administered after the seizure is important clinically since administering a drug after a seizure avoids the challenges of seizure prediction.
claims.source: Of particular note was nifedipine's inhibition of severe hypoxia even when administered after the seizure. Furthermore, this strategy is important clinically since administering a drug after a seizure avoids the challenges of seizure prediction.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing post-seizure nifedipine efficacy and speculation about clinical implications.

claims.claim: Most drugs, including anti-seizure medications, failed to modulate postictal severe hypoxia.
claims.source: Most drugs, including anti-seizure medications, failed to modulate this postictal severe hypoxia, which we believe emphasizes that this is a pathological phenomenon and that breakthrough seizures while on antiseizure medications do not directly protect against this insult.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from multiple drug treatments shown in Tables 3 and 4.

claims.claim: Breakthrough seizures while on antiseizure medications do not directly protect against postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia.
claims.source: Most drugs, including anti-seizure medications, failed to modulate this postictal severe hypoxia, which we believe emphasizes that this is a pathological phenomenon and that breakthrough seizures while on antiseizure medications do not directly protect against this insult.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lack of effect of ASDs on postictal hypoxia.

claims.claim: Postictal behavioral impairments last much longer than the seizures themselves and negatively impact quality of life.
claims.source: Postictal behavioral impairments last much longer than the seizures themselves and negatively impact quality of life.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established clinical knowledge about postictal impairments.

claims.claim: The mechanism underlying postictal behavioral disruptions were previously unknown and no treatment options existed.
claims.source: The mechanism underlying these disruptions were previously unknown and no treatment options existed.

claims.claim: Two common postictal impairments, Todd's paresis and amnesia, can be prevented by interfering with the pathways that lead to hypoperfusion/hypoxia.
claims.source: Our data clearly demonstrates that two common postictal impairments, Todd's paresis and amnesia, can be prevented by interfering with the pathways that lead to hypoperfusion/hypoxia.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data showing prevention of motor and memory impairments with nifedipine and acetaminophen.

claims.claim: L-type calcium antagonists and COX-2 inhibitors are strong candidates for the treatment of postictal behavioral impairments.
claims.source: Thus, L-type calcium antagonists and COX-2 inhibitors are strong candidates for the treatment of these currently untreated behavioral impairments.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the efficacy of these drugs in preventing postictal hypoxia and behavioral impairments.

claims.claim: Brief and mild seizures lead to an extended hypoperfusion/hypoxic event.
claims.source: Our discovery that brief and mild seizures lead to an extended hypoperfusion/hypoxic event is critically important because it establishes that seizures could injure the brain through postictal severe hypoxia, and not necessarily by the seizure itself.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from multiple seizure models showing postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia.

claims.claim: Seizures could injure the brain through postictal severe hypoxia, and not necessarily by the seizure itself.
claims.source: Our discovery that brief and mild seizures lead to an extended hypoperfusion/hypoxic event is critically important because it establishes that seizures could injure the brain through postictal severe hypoxia, and not necessarily by the seizure itself.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the discovery of postictal hypoxia and its potential consequences.

claims.claim: It is generally accepted that COX-2 inhibition is neuroprotective from seizures.
claims.source: Though there is some controversy (Rojas et al., 2014), it is generally accepted that COX-2 inhibition is neuroprotective from seizures.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rojas et al., 2014 and general knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: With genetic or pharmacological COX-2 inhibition, seizure-induced brain damage can be dramatically reduced.
claims.source: Indeed, with genetic or pharmacological COX-2 inhibition, seizure-induced brain damage can be dramatically reduced (Serrano et al., 2011; Kunz and Oliw, 2001; Hewett et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Serrano et al., 2011; Kunz and Oliw, 2001; Hewett et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Previous studies showing COX-2 inhibition reduces seizure-induced brain damage provided support for the hypothesis that postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia injures the brain.
claims.source: Though at the time of these studies researchers were unaware of postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia and the requirement of COX-2 in this response, they provided support for the hypothesis that postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia injures the brain.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference connecting previous findings about COX-2 neuroprotection to the current findings about postictal hypoxia.

claims.claim: Brain injury plays a central role in epileptogenesis.
claims.source: Given the central role of brain injury in epileptogenesis (Sloviter and Bumanglag, 2013), preventing injury from hypoperfusion/hypoxia may be a novel preventative treatment strategy in epilepsy.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sloviter and Bumanglag, 2013.

results.result: The authors establish 10 mmHg as the threshold for defining severe hypoxia based on prior literature showing that pO2 levels at or below this threshold cause significant cellular and physiological changes, brain injury, and worse clinical outcomes in various contexts including traumatic brain injury and tumor hypoxia.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 collectively establish the rationale for using 10 mmHg as the severe hypoxia threshold. The claims are well-supported by multiple independent citations (C3-C10) from diverse contexts (HIF-1 activation, ischemia, traumatic brain injury, tumor biology) that converge on this threshold. The baseline normoxia range (C1) provides appropriate context.

results.result: Seizures are followed by prolonged severe postictal hypoxia (pO2 < 10 mmHg) lasting approximately one hour, observed across multiple seizure models (spontaneous, kindled, MES, 3 Hz stimulation) and brain regions (hippocampus, neocortex), with severity positively correlated with seizure duration.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C21 demonstrate postictal hypoxia across multiple independent seizure models and measurement techniques (continuous oxygen monitoring, pimonidazole immunohistochemistry). The linear correlation between seizure duration and hypoxia severity (C15, R²=0.55, p<0.0001) and convergent evidence from different brain regions (C17-C18) strengthen the finding. The consistency across models (C19-C21) supports generalizability.

results.result: Postictal severe hypoxia is mediated by hypoperfusion and vasoconstriction, as demonstrated by concurrent blood flow measurements showing ~47% reduction in blood flow, direct observation of ~14% arteriole constriction in hippocampal slices, and prevention of both hypoxia and vasoconstriction by the L-type calcium channel blocker nifedipine.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C35 provide convergent evidence from multiple methodologies: laser Doppler flowmetry (C23, 53% of baseline flow), direct vessel diameter measurements in slices (C31, 13.8% constriction), and pharmacological validation with nifedipine (C25-C28, C33-C34). The Poiseuille's law calculation (C32) linking vessel diameter to flow is mathematically sound and correlates well with empirical measurements. The similar time-course of blood flow and oxygen recovery (C24) supports the causal relationship.

results.result: Postictal hypoperfusion occurs in human epilepsy patients, with 8 of 10 subjects showing cerebral blood flow reductions >10 mL/100 g/min (mean 26.6% reduction from baseline) that are spatially concordant with seizure localization and positively correlated with seizure duration.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C43 demonstrate clinical translation of the rodent findings using ASL-MRI. The quantitative measurements (C37-C38, C41) show substantial hypoperfusion, and the spatial concordance between hypoperfusion and seizure localization in all 8 positive cases (C42) supports specificity. The correlation with seizure duration (C39) parallels the rodent data (C15). The two negative cases (C40) are appropriately explained by shorter seizure durations, consistent with the dose-response relationship.

results.result: COX-2 activity during seizures is necessary for postictal severe hypoxia, as demonstrated by prevention of hypoxia with selective COX-2 inhibition (celecoxib) and dose-dependent inhibition with acetaminophen, but only when administered before or during (not after) seizures, and confirmed by prevention of vessel constriction in hippocampal slices.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C54 establish COX-2 as a key mediator through multiple lines of evidence: selective pharmacological inhibition (C47-C48), dose-response relationship with acetaminophen (C50), critical timing requirement (C51-C52), and direct vessel measurements in slices (C53-C54). The expression pattern (C44) and established role in neurovascular coupling (C45) provide mechanistic context. The lack of effect of COX-1 inhibition (C48) and the requirement for drug presence during seizures (C51-C52) support specificity.

results.result: Genetic evidence confirms COX-2's role in postictal hypoxia: PTGS2Y385F mice with impaired COX-2 cyclooxygenase activity do not develop postictal severe hypoxia despite normal seizure durations, and acetaminophen has no additional effect in these mutants while preventing hypoxia in wild-type controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 provide strong genetic validation of the pharmacological findings. The mutant mice (C55) have a specific point mutation affecting only cyclooxygenase activity while preserving peroxidase function, allowing precise mechanistic inference. The absence of hypoxia in mutants despite normal seizures (C56-C57) demonstrates necessity of COX-2 activity. The differential acetaminophen response (C58-C59) confirms target specificity and rules out off-target effects.

results.result: Postictal hypoperfusion/hypoxia is resistant to most vasodilatory treatments and commonly prescribed antiseizure drugs, with only COX-2 inhibition, L-type calcium channel blockade, and partial inhibition by PGE2 synthesis inhibition showing efficacy, highlighting the central roles of COX-2 activation and sustained calcium elevation in vascular smooth muscle.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C87, C109-C110 demonstrate the pharmacological profile through systematic testing of multiple drug classes (Tables 3-4). The lack of effect of most vasodilators (C82-C83) and ASDs (C85) emphasizes the pathological nature of the response. The partial effect of PGE2 synthesis inhibition (C109) and ethosuximide (C86-C87, which has some L-type calcium channel activity) support the proposed mechanism. The comprehensive negative results strengthen confidence in the positive findings.

results.result: Postictal severe hypoxia, not the seizure itself, causes Todd's paresis (motor weakness): nifedipine prevents both hypoxia and motor impairment without affecting seizure duration, motor deficits occur only during the hypoxic period (40 min post-seizure) and resolve when oxygen returns to normoxia (80 min).
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 demonstrate causality through pharmacological dissociation of seizures from hypoxia. The temporal correlation between hypoxia and motor deficit (C89), recovery coinciding with normoxia (C90), and prevention of both by nifedipine without affecting seizures (C88) provide strong evidence. The experimental design appropriately controls for seizure effects by showing that seizures without hypoxia do not cause motor impairment (C91).

results.result: Postictal severe hypoxia, not the seizure itself, causes memory impairment: rats experiencing hypoxia during memory encoding showed no preference for novel objects 24 hours later, while rats with seizures but prevented hypoxia (acetaminophen treatment) performed normally, demonstrating that hypoxia specifically disrupts memory formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 demonstrate causality for memory impairment using the same pharmacological dissociation strategy as for motor deficits. The novel object recognition task appropriately tests hippocampal-dependent memory. The lack of novelty preference in hypoxic rats (C92) indicates memory formation failure, while normal performance in acetaminophen-treated rats with seizures (C93) demonstrates that seizures alone do not impair memory. The convergence with motor deficit findings (C88-C91) strengthens the overall conclusion (C94).

results.result: Brief seizures initiate local, long-lasting hypoperfusion/hypoxic insults responsible for postictal behavioral dysfunction (Todd's paresis and amnesia), which can be prevented by interfering with hypoperfusion/hypoxia pathways, suggesting L-type calcium antagonists and COX-2 inhibitors as treatment candidates for currently untreated postictal impairments.
results.evaluation: Claims C95, C114-C117 synthesize the major findings into a coherent conclusion supported by the behavioral experiments (C88-C94) and mechanistic studies (C22-C59). The clinical context (C114-C115) establishes significance. The therapeutic proposal (C116-C117) is appropriately cautious ('candidates') and directly follows from the experimental evidence showing prevention of both hypoxia and behavioral deficits.

results.result: The authors resolve prior conflicting reports of postictal hemodynamic changes (hypoperfusion vs. hyperperfusion) by demonstrating that timing of measurement is critical: severe hypoxia occurs between 20-60 min post-seizure in rats, and only previous studies imaging during this window observed hypoperfusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C100 appropriately contextualize the findings within prior literature. The explanation for discordant results (C97) is logical and supported by the time-course data (C98) and selective citation analysis (C99). The clinical implication for seizure localization (C100) is reasonable speculation supported by a citation. This represents good scientific practice in reconciling conflicting literature.

results.result: Previous studies identified only a brief ictal oxygen 'dip' that quickly recovers, missing the prolonged postictal hypoxia due to short recording durations (≤30 s post-seizure) and use of ketamine anesthesia which inhibits NMDA-dependent COX-2 activation; the prolonged postictal hypoxia likely accounts for previously observed hypoxyprobe labeling attributed to ictal hypoxia.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C106 appropriately address why postictal hypoxia was not previously identified. The citations to prior work (C101-C102, C105) are accurate, and the explanation involving ketamine's effects on COX-2 (C103-C104) is mechanistically sound and supported by citation. The reinterpretation of hypoxyprobe data (C105-C106) is reasonable given the magnitude and duration differences between ictal and postictal hypoxia.

results.result: Under normal conditions, COX-2 mediates vasodilation for neurovascular coupling, but during pathophysiological seizure activity, this system switches to produce prolonged vasoconstriction, representing a pathological reversal of normal neurovascular coupling mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 provide important mechanistic context. The normal role of COX-2 in vasodilation (C107) is well-established by citations. The observation of reversal to vasoconstriction during seizures (C108) is supported by the blood flow and vessel diameter data (C22-C35). This represents a novel insight into how normal physiological mechanisms can become pathological.

results.result: Nifedipine's efficacy when administered post-seizure is clinically important as it avoids seizure prediction challenges; most drugs including antiseizure medications failed to prevent postictal hypoxia, indicating breakthrough seizures on ASDs do not protect against this insult.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 highlight clinically relevant findings. The post-seizure efficacy of nifedipine (C111) is supported by data (C28) and the clinical reasoning is sound. The systematic testing of ASDs (C112, Table 4) provides important negative results with clinical implications. The inference about breakthrough seizures (C113) is logical and clinically relevant.

results.result: Brief seizures lead to extended hypoperfusion/hypoxic events that could injure the brain independently of seizure activity itself; previous studies showing COX-2 inhibition reduces seizure-induced brain damage may have been preventing hypoperfusion/hypoxia injury, suggesting that preventing this injury may be a novel preventative strategy in epileptogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C124 propose an important hypothesis linking postictal hypoxia to brain injury and epileptogenesis. While the discovery of postictal hypoxia (C118) is well-supported, the causal link to brain injury (C119) remains speculative. The reinterpretation of prior COX-2 neuroprotection studies (C120-C122) is plausible but indirect. The therapeutic speculation (C124) is reasonable but requires validation. This represents appropriate hypothesis generation for future work rather than demonstrated results.
